title: Delete and rename files the way git understands
summary: Git does not store renames. It infers them. Learn what git rm and git mv actually do, and why a rename plus an edit sometimes shows up as a delete and an add.
mental_model: There is no rename in git's data model — only trees of paths pointing at content. `git mv` is delete-plus-add staged together, and `git log` reconstructs the rename afterwards by noticing the content barely changed.

steps.title: Delete a file the way git wants
steps.why: `git rm` removes it from disk AND stages the deletion in one step. Deleting in your file manager works too, but leaves you to remember `git add -A` afterwards.
steps.expect: D staged in the left column, with no separate add needed.

steps.title: Untrack without deleting
steps.why: `--cached` stages the removal but leaves the file on disk. This is how you stop tracking a file you still need locally — config, secrets, a big local fixture. Untracking without also ignoring it is only half the job: the next `git add -A` would put it straight back.
steps.expect: notes.txt is untracked and ignored, and still sitting on disk.

steps.title: Rename with git mv
steps.why: `git mv` moves the file and stages both halves. Git records a delete of the old path and an add of the new one — the word 'rename' appears only later, when something reconstructs it.
steps.expect: Status is smart enough to already call it a rename.

steps.title: Commit and watch git infer the rename
steps.why: `--stat` says 'old_name.py => dosing.py'. Nothing in the commit object says rename; git compared the blobs, found them identical, and reported it. That inference is why renames are free in git.
commands: git commit -m "Rename dosing module, drop legacy code"

verify.label: the commit reads as a rename

steps.title: Break the inference on purpose
steps.why: Rename plus heavy edit in one commit drops the similarity below the threshold, and git reports a delete and an add instead. History becomes harder to follow — which is why you rename in one commit and edit in the next.
commands: git commit -m "Rewrite dosing as chemistry module"
steps.expect: A delete and an add, no arrow — the content changed too much.

steps.title: Make git look harder
steps.why: `-M` lowers the similarity threshold, so git will call something a rename even after a heavy edit. `--follow` traces one path backwards through renames. Both are read-time flags — history did not change, only how hard you asked git to look.
steps.expect: With -M20% the arrow comes back. Compare it with the plain --stat from the previous step.

verify.label: the deleted and renamed paths are gone from tracking
verify.hint: git rm legacy.py, git rm --cached notes.txt (and ignore it), git mv old_name.py …

verify.label: the renamed module is tracked under its new name
notes.txt is untracked but still on disk — that is what --cached does
the pure rename was detected as a rename
verify.hint: git mv on its own commit keeps history readable

verify.label: the rename-plus-rewrite was NOT detected — it reads as a delete and an add
verify.hint: that is the lesson: rename in one commit, rewrite in the next

pitfalls: On a case-insensitive filesystem, `git mv readme.md README.md` may be ignored. Use `git mv -f`, or rename via a temporary name.
Renaming and rewriting a file in the same commit hides the rename from history. Split them into two commits.
`git rm -r --cached .` unstages the entire repo. It is the classic 'fix my .gitignore' incantation, and it is easy to fire by accident.
`git mv` is only a convenience. Renaming in your editor and running `git add -A` produces an identical commit.
cheatsheet: delete from disk and stage the deletion
detect renames when reading a commit
